name: Blue Book Retail Concept Model
description: The worked example from the Blue Book, an Agile Data Guide to Modeling Business Concepts by Juha Korpela and Shane Gibson: a retailer that sells products through a website and physical stores, modeled from order to delivery.

concepts.name: Customer
concepts.description: A Customer is a person or organisation that has placed at least one Sales Order with us, through any Channel.
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: has placed at least one Sales Order with us
examples: A shopper who bought a kettle on the website last week
A café that orders cups from the store every month
Fact: Customer 'Harbour Café' places Sales Order 'SO-1042'.
specialCases: Someone with an account and no Sales Orders is a prospect, not a Customer
A Customer who buys on the website and in a store is one Customer, not two

concepts.name: Channel
concepts.description: A Channel is a way a Customer can place a Sales Order with us.
examples: Fact: Sales Order 'SO-1042' is placed via Channel 'Website'.
specialCases: A phone call taken in a store is placed through that store
A courier is not a Channel. It carries Deliveries, it does not take Sales Orders
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: a Customer can place a Sales Order with us

concepts.name: Sales Order
concepts.description: A Sales Order is a Customer's request to buy one or many Products, placed through one Channel.
examples: An order for a kettle and two mugs placed on the website this morning
A café's monthly order for cups, placed in the store
Fact: Sales Order 'SO-1042' is placed for Product 'Box of cups'.
specialCases: A Sales Order can be fulfilled by more than one Delivery when the Products ship separately
A Sales Order the Customer cancels before any Delivery is still a Sales Order, with nothing delivered
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: a Customer makes to buy one or many Products, through one Channel

concepts.name: Product
concepts.description: A Product is a thing we sell to Customers and buy from Suppliers.
specialCases: The items on the shelf are Products, the count of them is Stock
A red kettle and a blue kettle are two Products when we keep and sell them separately
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: we sell to Customers and buy from Suppliers

concepts.name: Stock
concepts.description: Stock is the quantity of a Product held in a Warehouse.
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: counts one Product held in one Warehouse
examples: Forty kettles in the main warehouse this morning
specialCases: Stock is the count, not the items, the items are Products
Kettles loaded on a Delivery van are no longer Stock in the Warehouse

concepts.name: Supplier
concepts.description: A Supplier is an organisation we buy Products from to restock our Warehouses.
examples: Fact: Supplier 'Kitchenware Wholesale' receives Purchase Order 'PO-0201'.
specialCases: A Supplier that also buys from us is still a Supplier when it receives a Purchase Order
A company we have never sent a Purchase Order to is not yet a Supplier
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: we buy Products from to restock our Warehouses

concepts.name: Purchase Order
concepts.description: A Purchase Order is our request to a Supplier for one or many Products, raised by an Employee to restock.
examples: A Purchase Order for two hundred kettles raised when Stock ran low
A weekly Purchase Order to the wholesaler for cups and mugs
specialCases: A Purchase Order we cancel before the Supplier ships is still a Purchase Order
Sending faulty Products back to a Supplier is a return, not a Purchase Order
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: we send to a Supplier for one or many Products, to restock

concepts.name: Warehouse
concepts.description: A Warehouse is a place where we hold Stock and dispatch Deliveries from.
specialCases: A store's back room that ships online orders counts as a Warehouse
A store that only sells over the counter is not a Warehouse

concepts.name: Warehouse Physical Location
concepts.description: A Warehouse Physical Location is the address a Warehouse sits at.
examples: A unit on the industrial park at the edge of town
Fact: Warehouse 'Main' is located in Warehouse Physical Location 'Bedford'.
specialCases: When a Warehouse moves, it gets a new Warehouse Physical Location
One Warehouse Physical Location holds one Warehouse on this Map

concepts.name: Customer Delivery Location
concepts.description: A Customer Delivery Location is a place a Customer has asked us to deliver to.
examples: Fact: Customer 'Harbour Café' has Customer Delivery Location 'Back door, 12 Quay Street'.
specialCases: A Customer can have several, home and work
A store where a Customer collects an order is not a Customer Delivery Location
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: a Customer has asked us to deliver to

concepts.name: Delivery
concepts.description: A Delivery is one trip that takes Products from a Warehouse to a Customer Delivery Location.
examples: Two mugs delivered to a home address on Tuesday
Cups for the café, delivered to its back door on Friday
specialCases: One Sales Order can arrive in several Deliveries, and one Delivery can carry several Sales Orders
A van run with three stops is three Deliveries, one for each Customer Delivery Location
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: takes Products from a Warehouse to a Customer Delivery Location

concepts.name: Employee
concepts.description: An Employee is a person who works for us and does the work in this Scope.
examples: Catherine, who raises the Purchase Orders
A driver who delivers to Customers
specialCases: A contractor who delivers for us is treated as an Employee on this Map
A Supplier's driver who drops off Products is not an Employee
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: works for us and does the work in this Scope

concepts.name: Team
concepts.description: A Team is a group of Employees who do the work together, led by one Employee.
specialCases: An Employee is a member of one Team at a time
A group that meets for one project is not a Team
concepts.definitionDifferentiator: do the work together, led by one Employee

coreBusinessEvents.name: Customer places a Sales Order for one or many Products via a Channel
Employee raises a Purchase Order for one or many Products with a Supplier
Product is restocked into a Warehouse
coreBusinessEvents.notes: Who makes the restock happen is still an open question in the book.

coreBusinessEvents.name: Employee delivers one or many Products from a Warehouse to a Customer Delivery Location
Employee is assigned to lead a Team

domains.name: Sales
domains.description: Customers placing Sales Orders through a Channel, the website or a store.

domains.name: Inventory
domains.description: Products, the Stock held of them in Warehouses, and the Purchase Orders raised with Suppliers to restock.

domains.name: Fulfilment
domains.description: Deliveries that take Products from a Warehouse to a Customer Delivery Location.

domains.name: Human Resources
domains.description: The Employees and Teams doing the work, and nothing more of HR.

scope.statement: Order to delivery for a retailer that sells products through a website and physical stores: customers placing orders, warehouses holding and restocking stock, and employees delivering to the customer. Not finance, not marketing, not HR beyond the people doing the work.

participants.name: Retail Operations Manager
participants.notes: Has run stores, managed the warehouse roster, and chased more late deliveries than she cares to remember

stories.name: A customer places an order
stories.text: A customer places an order for one or many products through a channel, the website or a store. They pay for it. The warehouse picks the products and an employee delivers them to the customer's delivery location. When stock runs low, an employee raises a purchase order with a supplier, and the stock gets restocked into a warehouse.

stories.name: Stock runs low and gets restocked
stories.text: Every morning we check the stock of each product in each warehouse. When a product runs low, an employee raises a purchase order with the supplier for that product. The supplier receives the purchase order and ships the products, and they are restocked into the warehouse.

stories.name: A customer returns part of a delivery
stories.text: An order arrives in two deliveries because one product shipped from the other warehouse. The customer keeps the first delivery but returns part of the second one.

stories.name: An employee is assigned to lead a team
stories.text: Every employee is a member of a team. When a team needs a new lead, the operations manager assigns one of its employees to lead it.

businessQuestions.name: How many Sales Orders were placed through each Channel last month?
How often do Deliveries miss the promised date?
How long does a Restock take, from Purchase Order to Stock on the shelf?
What is the margin per Product per Channel?
